aiGenerationNote:

Guide the user through using `journalctl -f`, `mailq`, and `postconf -n` to diagnose the problem. screens.title: Troubleshooting Email Services and Log Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Email stacks combine transport, delivery agents, authentication, and filtering. When mail fails, logs and simple client simulations are your fastest path to a root cause. In this lesson you will learn how to read Postfix and Dovecot events, use systemd journal tools to filter mail output, run Postfix utilities to inspect the queue and configuration, and simulate SMTP and IMAP sessions with telnet and openssl. You will also learn why DNS records like MX, A, SPF, DKIM and DMARC matter for deliverability and reputation. Throughout we emphasize practical commands you can run on a server: journalctl, mailq and postqueue, postconf, postlog, telnet, openssl s_client, and dig. You will see a hands-on scenario where a removed mydestination entry causes local delivery to fail, and how logs plus mailq guide the fix. By the end, you will have a checklist you can apply during incidents: locate the right logs, reproduce a session with a client tool, check the queue and configuration, and confirm DNS and filtering services are healthy. Ready to make logs work for you?

Troubleshooting Email Services

Identify, reproduce, and fix delivery, authentication, and filtering problems using logs and CLI tools.

Estimate: 15 minute lab
In this lesson

Log analysis with journalctl, Postfix/Dovecot logs, queue inspection, simulated SMTP/IMAP sessions, and DNS checks for deliverability.

Coming up

A hands-on scenario where a misconfigured mydestination causes local delivery to fail and how to fix it by reading logs and updating main.cf.

Simulate sessions

Simulated connections

Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

Skill-based goals tied to troubleshooting workflows and verification milestones.

Bloom: Learn → Understand → Apply → Master
01 Identify mail logs
Locate Postfix, Dovecot, and Amavisd logs and why each is useful.

Knowing which file or journal unit to inspect reduces noise and speeds diagnosis. Matching log types to symptoms prevents chasing unrelated events.

Verified Competency Milestone
02 Use journalctl effectively
Filter mail units, follow in real-time, and search for error keywords.

Journalctl gives structured access to systemd logs; learning to combine unit filters and grep-like searches isolates relevant entries quickly.

Verified Competency Milestone
03 Inspect queue & config
Use mailq, postqueue, postsuper, and postconf to view queue and settings.

Queue inspection reveals delivery errors and transient conditions; configuration checks confirm intended routing and delivery behavior.

Verified Competency Milestone
04 Simulate client sessions
Use telnet and openssl s_client to reproduce SMTP/IMAP behavior and TLS negotiation.

Simulating the protocol is the quickest way to separate client misconfiguration from server-side failures and TLS certificate issues.

Verified Competency Milestone

Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Learning Objectives

Practice Milestones

Complete the following applied tasks to demonstrate troubleshooting fluency.

05 Diagnose outgoing delivery
Resolve 'Host not found' by checking DNS resolution and network reachability.

Check /etc/resolv.conf, run dig for MX and A records, and confirm firewall rules permit outbound SMTP on port 25.

Verified Competency Milestone
06 Fix local delivery mishaps
Restore correct mydestination and verify mail reaches maildirs.

Use journalctl output and mailq to find bounce reasons, edit main.cf, reload Postfix, and re-test delivery.

Verified Competency Milestone
07 Check authentication failures
Diagnose Dovecot login errors and mailbox path or permission issues.

Search Dovecot logs for 'authentication failed' and verify user entries and plaintext-auth settings where necessary.

Verified Competency Milestone
08 Verify DNS & anti-abuse records
Confirm SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are present to improve deliverability.

These DNS records do not live in Postfix, but missing or incorrect entries often cause rejections or downstream mailbox filtering.

Verified Competency Milestone

screens.title: Logs: The First Line of Defense
screens.narratorSegment: Logs are your primary diagnostic source when mail misbehaves. On systemd-based distributions journalctl is the default interface; older Red Hat systems may still use /var/log/maillog. Postfix prefixes indicate the subsystem generating entries — for example postfix/smtpd shows incoming SMTP activity, postfix/qmgr shows queue operations, and postfix/smtp shows outgoing delivery attempts. Dovecot records authentication and mailbox delivery messages, and Amavisd-new logs provide spam and virus scan results. Start by narrowing time ranges and unit names: sudo journalctl -u postfix -n 50 shows the last 50 Postfix entries and sudo journalctl -u dovecot -n 50 shows recent Dovecot activity. When following live output use -f. A concrete example: if you see status=deferred with a host lookup failure, that points immediately to DNS or network reachability rather than mailbox permissions. A common misconception is scanning maillog for keywords without context; instead, correlate timestamps, queue IDs, and consecutive events to build a timeline of what the MTA tried. Always capture the queue ID from the log and then use mailq to inspect related queue lines. In short, learn the suffixes, use unit filters, and correlate queue IDs to move quickly from symptom to root cause. What timeline will you build on your next incident?

keyIdea.title: Correlate Timestamps & Queue IDs
keyIdea.text: Use unit filters and queue IDs in logs to trace a message's path from reception to delivery or failure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Log Analysis
Definition

Logs and journalctl usage

Use journalctl filters and legacy maillog to isolate Postfix, Dovecot, and Amavisd events. Correlate queue IDs and timestamps.

Common commands
sudo journalctl -u postfix -n 50
sudo journalctl -u postfix -f
sudo journalctl -u dovecot -n 50
sudo journalctl -u amavisd -n 50
sudo tail -f /var/log/maillog
Example observation
If log shows status=deferred with host lookup errors, suspect DNS or resolver issues rather than mailbox problems.
Common mistake
Reading isolated errors without following the queue ID can mislead you about the true cause.
Practical tip

Correlate log lines to queue entries

  • Capture the Postfix queue ID from a log line and run mailq to match delivery attempts.
  • Use journalctl -u --since "10 minutes ago" to limit output to the incident window.
  • Follow logs live to reproduce a failure while you resend a test message.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Logs show what the service tried; combine timestamps and queue IDs to reconstruct the message path.

screens.title: Reading Postfix Subsystem Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Postfix writes different log prefixes for each subsystem; learning to read those prefixes is critical. postfix/smtpd covers incoming SMTP sessions and command-level responses. When you see rejected connections or authentication errors, smtpd entries are where to start. postfix/qmgr logs queue manager actions such as enqueueing and handing messages to delivery agents. postfix/smtp shows outbound delivery attempts to remote hosts and records SMTP responses from remote MTAs; when you see 4xx or 5xx codes in these entries, they explain why Postfix deferred or bounced mail. postfix/local or postfix/pipe indicate local delivery via the local MTA or an external delivery program like the Dovecot LDA. Practical workflow: reproduce the error, note the queue ID, then run sudo journalctl -u postfix | grep ' ' to gather all related lines. Example commands shown in the visual include tailing the unit and filtering for 'reject' or 'status=deferred'. A misconception is assuming all 'reject' messages are permanent when some are transient 4xx responses; check timestamps and retry behavior. Use the queue ID to link Postfix logs to mailq output and to decide whether to force a queue flush or remove deferred messages. How will you use the queue ID to triangulate the cause on your next ticket?

keyIdea.title: Match Subsystem to Symptom
keyIdea.text: Use the Postfix prefix to immediately direct investigation to incoming, queue, outbound, or local delivery issues.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Postfix Logs
Process Flow

Subsystem mapping

  • postfix/smtpd — incoming SMTP sessions and command responses.
  • postfix/qmgr — queue manager, enqueue and handoffs to delivery agents.
  • postfix/smtp — outbound deliveries and remote SMTP responses.
  • postfix/local / postfix/pipe — local delivery and external delivery agents like dovecot-lda.
Commands & filters
sudo journalctl -u postfix -n 50
sudo journalctl -u postfix -f
sudo journalctl -u postfix | grep "reject" | less
sudo journalctl -u postfix | grep ""
Example
If you see a line with 'status=deferred' and a 450 response in postfix/smtp, the remote host returned a temporary error. Retry or investigate network/DNS reachability.
Common misconception
Treating all 'reject' entries as permanent. Check the numeric SMTP code (4xx vs 5xx) — 4xx is temporary and often resolves, 5xx is permanent and needs content or routing fixes.
Key Takeaway

Match the Postfix subsystem to the observed symptom and use queue IDs to correlate across logs and mailq output.

screens.title: Dovecot: Authentication and Delivery Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Dovecot logs give you visibility into authentication, IMAP/POP3 session activity, and local delivery handoffs. When users cannot log in, Dovecot is usually the place to look for exact failure messages such as 'authentication failed' or 'user not found'. Start with sudo journalctl -u dovecot -n 50 and search the output for authentication keywords. Also confirm that the mailbox path exists and permissions are correct; missing or misowned Maildirs will appear as delivery or access errors. A concrete example: a user reports login failures; you grep the dovecot journal and find 'authentication failed' followed by a reason like 'user not found in passwd-file'. That points you toward the authentication backend rather than network issues. A common misconception is to blame the mail client immediately — always verify the server-side authentication log first. For delivery, Dovecot may be invoked as the LDA; check for dovecot-lda handoff messages and any errors indicating mailbox creation or permission denial. After addressing the root cause, test a login with telnet or openssl to reproduce the successful authentication. The key is matching the error text to the authentication backend and mailbox state so you can apply the right fix.

keyIdea.title: Server-Side First
keyIdea.text: When auth or delivery fails, check Dovecot logs and mailbox state before adjusting client configuration.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Dovecot Logs
Definition

Authentication and delivery traces

Use Dovecot logs to identify authentication backends, reasons for failure, and mailbox delivery or permission errors.

Useful commands
sudo journalctl -u dovecot -n 50
sudo journalctl -u dovecot -f
sudo journalctl -u dovecot | grep "authentication failed"
Example: 'authentication failed' followed by 'user not found in passwd-file' points to the authentication backend or virtual user database rather than network connectivity.
Checklist
  • Confirm user exists in the configured authentication backend.
  • Verify mailbox path and ownership (Maildir exists and is accessible).
  • Check disable_plaintext_auth and TLS requirements when testing with clients.
Pro tip
Use a short reproducer: connect with openssl s_client or telnet, attempt a login, and observe the dovecot journal simultaneously to capture the exact failure text.
Key Takeaway

Dovecot logs show the authentication reason—backend mismatches and mailbox permissions are frequent root causes.

screens.title: Spam and Virus Filtering Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Filtering components sit between Postfix and local delivery; amavisd-new logs reveal whether messages are flagged as spam or infected. If users report missing mail or unexpected quarantines, check amavisd logs: sudo journalctl -u amavisd -n 50 and search for 'SPAM' or virus detections. Filtering failures can be caused by service downtime, misconfigured content_filter entries in Postfix's main. cf or master. cf, or stale virus definitions. A practical check sequence: confirm amavisd, SpamAssassin and ClamAV are running; look for communication entries between Postfix and Amavisd; ensure content filter transport (typically on port 10025) is present. Run freshclam to update virus signatures if ClamAV is out of date. A common misconception is assuming filtering problems always mean spam rules need tweaking — often the issue is an IPC failure between Postfix and the filter or a stopped filter process. Use the logs to see whether messages are passed through, tagged, or rejected, and correlate that with Postfix entries referencing the content_filter transport. When debugging, tail both postfix and amavisd logs together while injecting a test message so you can observe the filter handoff and result in sequence.

keyIdea.title: Filter Handoffs are Visible
keyIdea.text: Check both MTA and filter logs; tags and transport names reveal whether messages were scanned, quarantined, or passed.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Amavisd-new & Filtering
Definition

Filtering visibility

Amavisd and scanning services log spam and virus detections; Postfix shows handoffs via content_filter and transports like 10025.

Commands
sudo journalctl -u amavisd -n 50
sudo journalctl -u amavisd | grep "SPAM"
sudo systemctl status spamassassin clamav-daemon amavisd
sudo freshclam
Troubleshooting steps
  1. Check amavisd logs for detection and transport handoff messages.
  2. Confirm content_filter entries in Postfix main.cf and master.cf for the proper port (often 10025).
  3. Ensure SpamAssassin and ClamAV are running and updated with freshclam.
Common misconception: blaming content rules first. Always verify inter-service connectivity and service status before altering filtering rules.
Key Takeaway

Filter failures are often service or handoff issues; logs show whether a message was scanned, tagged, or dropped.

screens.title: mailq, postqueue, postsuper, postconf, and postlog
screens.narratorSegment: Postfix ships utilities that let you inspect current queue state, flush or remove messages, and query configuration. mailq or sudo postqueue -p shows queued messages and the reason for deferral or bounce; you will typically see the queue ID and a short status reason like 'Host not found'. If you must remove deferred mail, postsuper -d ALL deferred clears it — use this cautiously in production. Use sudo postqueue -f to force a queue flush after you fix a network or DNS issue. For configuration, postconf -n shows only non-default settings, which helps you confirm intentional overrides. You can query a single parameter with postconf myhostname, and postconf -d shows default values. postlog is handy when testing scripts or log rotation; it injects a message into Postfix logs so you can confirm log handling. Concrete command examples appear in the code panel: mailq, postqueue -f, postsuper -d ALL deferred, postconf -n and postlog -t mytest. A common misconception is assuming removing deferred mail hides the root cause — always identify why mail deferred before mass-deleting. When you use these tools, capture queue IDs and pair them with journalctl output to create a complete incident timeline.

keyIdea.title: Use Queue Tools Carefully
keyIdea.text: Inspect the queue to learn the failure reason; only delete or flush the queue after understanding the root cause.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Postfix Utilities
Code Walkthrough

Queue and config commands

mailq
sudo postqueue -p
sudo postsuper -d ALL deferred     # careful: deletes deferred messages
sudo postqueue -f                   # force queue flush

postconf -n                         # show non-default parameters
postconf myhostname                 # show specific parameter
postconf -d                         # show defaults

sudo postlog -t mytest "This is a test log entry from postlog."
Use mailq to read the queue and pair queue IDs with journalctl lines. Use postconf -n to spot non-default routing or filtering settings introduced by administrators or automation.
Scenario
If many messages show 'Host not found', do not delete the queue immediately. First fix DNS or resolver, then run postqueue -f to retry deliveries.
Common mistake: running postsuper -d ALL deferred without preserving evidence. Capture logs and queue snapshots before destructive actions.
Key Takeaway

Postfix utilities let you inspect and act on the queue and configuration — pair them with logs before any destructive change.

screens.title: telnet and openssl s_client for SMTP/IMAP Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Manual protocol sessions isolate client-server protocol steps and expose where negotiation fails. For SMTP you can use telnet to port 25 or 587 and type EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA and QUIT to simulate a send. Watch for server responses like 250 OK or 5xx permanent failures. For TLS validation use openssl s_client: openssl s_client -connect mail. example. com:25 -starttls smtp will perform a STARTTLS handshake, letting you inspect the certificate chain and cipher selection. For SMTPS on port 465, use openssl s_client -connect mail. example. com:465 -crlf. For IMAP use telnet to 143 or openssl s_client to 993 for IMAPS. A concrete example: if your client sees a TLS handshake failure, openssl s_client will display certificate errors and the server's presented chain; this confirms whether the issue is client trust or server certificate misconfiguration. A misconception is that telnet hides TLS-related failures — telnet shows cleartext protocol exchange but cannot test STARTTLS unless you then use openssl. Use both tools in sequence: telnet to confirm plain SMTP conversation, then openssl to validate TLS negotiation. When you simulate commands, record the exact server responses and correlate them to the Postfix logs to complete the diagnostic loop.

keyIdea.title: Reproduce the Protocol
keyIdea.text: Simulating SMTP/IMAP sessions reveals the precise server response codes and TLS handshake issues so you can map them to log entries.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Simulated Connections
Code Walkthrough

SMTP and TLS tests

telnet mail.example.com 25
# EHLO your_client.com
# MAIL FROM:
# RCPT TO:
# DATA
# Subject: Test
#
# This is a test message.
# .
# QUIT

# STARTTLS test
openssl s_client -connect mail.example.com:25 -starttls smtp -crlf
# SMTPS test
openssl s_client -connect mail.example.com:465 -crlf
Record numeric SMTP responses. A 250 indicates success; 5xx indicates permanent failure. Use openssl to inspect certificates when TLS is involved.
IMAP checks
telnet mail.example.com 143
# a1 LOGIN username password
# a2 LIST "" "*"
# a3 LOGOUT

# IMAPS
openssl s_client -connect mail.example.com:993 -crlf
Example: openssl s_client will print certificate validation errors. If the server presents a chain missing intermediates, remote MTAs or clients may reject your STARTTLS attempt.
Key Takeaway

Use telnet for protocol-level reproduction and openssl s_client for TLS handshakes; both are essential to isolate client vs server issues.

screens.title: Outgoing Mail Stuck: Host not found
screens.narratorSegment: When outgoing messages show 'Host not found' in the queue, Postfix cannot resolve the recipient's mail host. The most likely cause is a DNS resolver issue on the mail server. Immediate steps: check /etc/resolv. conf for valid nameserver entries, test DNS with dig MX recipient_domain. com and dig A mail. recipient_domain. com from the mail host, and confirm network connectivity to your configured DNS servers. Also check firewall rules that might block outbound DNS queries or SMTP connections. In practice, reproduce the failure by sending a message, run mailq to capture the queue ID and reason, then inspect journalctl -u postfix for matching lines that show name resolution failure. If DNS resolution succeeds from the server but Postfix still shows host lookup failures, verify that chroot or containerized environments have access to resolv. conf and that DNS is reachable from the Postfix process. A misconception is to assume Postfix is misconfigured; often the resolver is unreachable or mis-specified. After fixing resolv. conf or network access, run postqueue -f to retry deliveries. This stepwise approach isolates network/DNS versus MTA configuration issues and guides a targeted fix.

keyIdea.text: Host not found errors typically indicate resolver or network issues; verify DNS and connectivity before changing MTA settings.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Outgoing Delivery
Process

Diagnose 'Host not found'

  1. Run mailq to capture queue IDs and status messages.
  2. Check journalctl -u postfix | grep '' for name resolution lines.
  3. Verify /etc/resolv.conf and test with dig MX recipient_domain.com.
  4. Confirm network access to DNS servers and port 25 outbound firewall rules.
Commands
mailq
sudo journalctl -u postfix | grep "Host not found"
cat /etc/resolv.conf
dig MX recipient_domain.com
dig A mail.recipient_domain.com
sudo postqueue -f
Common misconception: changing Postfix routing settings before confirming DNS will mask the real network issue and risk misrouting messages.
Key Takeaway

When Postfix reports host lookup failures, treat DNS and resolver reachability as primary suspects and verify before changing MTA settings.

screens.title: Lab: Diagnose and Fix mydestination Misconfiguration
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through a realistic local delivery failure caused by removing $mydomain from mydestination. First, modify /etc/postfix/main. cf to remove $mydomain and reload Postfix. Send a test email to a local user and observe failure. Use sudo journalctl -u postfix -n 50 --no-pager and mailq to capture the queue ID and error; you should see entries indicating 'mail for your_domain. com loops back to myself' or 'unknown user' depending on configuration. The repair is to add $mydomain back to mydestination in main. cf, reload Postfix with sudo systemctl reload postfix, then resend the message. Verify success by checking journalctl for status=sent (delivered via dovecot-lda) or similar successful delivery messages. A common misconception is restarting Dovecot immediately—this step is unnecessary if the failure stems from mydestination. Use postconf -n before and after your change to confirm the effective configuration. This lab teaches you to combine a targeted configuration edit with log correlation and queue inspection rather than broad restarts or destructive queue deletions. After completing the steps, reflect on what log lines pointed most clearly to the misconfiguration.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Hands-on Activity
Scenario

Simulate incorrect mydestination

Remove $mydomain from mydestination, reload Postfix, send a local email, and use logs and mailq to diagnose and fix.

Example edit
# /etc/postfix/main.cf
mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost
# REMOVED: $mydomain
Verification commands
sudo systemctl reload postfix
echo "This email should fail local delivery." | mail -s "Troubleshooting Test" mailuser1@your_domain.com
sudo journalctl -u postfix -n 50 --no-pager
mailq
postconf -n
Fix
# Restore main.cf
mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, localhost, $mydomain
sudo systemctl reload postfix
# Resend test
echo "This email should now deliver successfully." | mail -s "Troubleshooting Fix Test" mailuser1@your_domain.com
sudo journalctl -u postfix | grep "status=sent"
Expected: first send appears in mailq with an error; after fix and reload, the message is delivered and logs show status=sent with delivery via dovecot-lda.
Key Takeaway

Controlled misconfigurations teach systematic diagnosis: reproduce, inspect logs and queue, apply a minimal fix, and verify the outcome.

screens.title: IMAP/POP3 Login Issues and Dovecot
screens.narratorSegment: When a user cannot log in, you must decide whether the problem originates on the server or in the client. Server-side signs include 'authentication failed' or 'user not found' in Dovecot logs, missing Maildir directories, or incorrect ownership and permissions on mailbox paths. Client-side signs can include authentication errors only from a single client or unusual client-side TLS errors. A practical path: check Dovecot logs first for explicit reasons; if logs say user not found, inspect password backends and virtual user files. If logs show permission denied, inspect Maildir paths and fix ownership. If the server log shows nothing, reproduce the login via telnet or openssl s_client while tailing the dovecot journal to capture the server's reaction. Also check disable_plaintext_auth settings and TLS requirements; some clients fail if plaintext auth is disabled without TLS. A common misconception is to reset the user's password before verifying the actual failure reason; instead, gather evidence from logs and simulate the authentication to confirm the root cause. Finish by testing a successful login and confirming delivery or mailbox listing to validate the repair. IMAP/POP3 Login Issues and Dovecot means use dovecot logs and simulated logins to determine whether to adjust authentication backends, mailbox permissions, or client settings.. In practical terms, differentiate server-side auth issues from client configuration problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › Authentication Failures
Comparison

Server vs Client indicators

Server: explicit 'authentication failed' or 'user not found' in dovecot logs; check backend and user store.
Client: TLS errors or failures only from a single client; ask the user to test a different client or device.
Delivery: if authentication succeeds but Maildir is absent or permissions incorrect, you will see delivery errors in logs.
Commands to reproduce
sudo journalctl -u dovecot -n 50 | grep "authentication failed"
# Reproduce auth while tailing logs
openssl s_client -connect mail.example.com:993 -crlf
# Or telnet for non-TLS demo
telnet mail.example.com 143
# Attempt: a1 LOGIN username password
Common mistake: resetting passwords without checking logs. The right fix follows from evidence: backend lookup, permission error, or TLS requirement.
Key Takeaway

Confirm the server's log message before acting. Reproduce the auth while tailing logs to capture the decisive error text.

screens.title: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC — Why DNS Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond MX and A records, SPF, DKIM and DMARC play a decisive role in whether your mail is accepted or marked as spam. SPF is a DNS TXT record that lists which hosts are allowed to send mail for your domain; it helps recipient servers quickly determine if a sending IP is authorized. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages so the recipient can verify the email's origin and integrity using a published public key. DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM by declaring a policy that tells receivers what to do when a message fails authentication and allows you to request reports. These records are not configured inside Postfix or Dovecot directly but are essential verification checkpoints for remote MTAs. A common misconception is treating these as optional; without them your outgoing mail is more likely to be soft- or hard-rejected or silently routed to spam. Practical checks include dig TXT example. com to find SPF or DKIM selectors and verifying that DKIM public keys match the signing selector. If delivery fails despite correct MTA logs, confirm these DNS records with the receiving domain’s rejection messages. In short: DNS proves who you are; ensure these records are present and correct as part of your incident checklist.

keyIdea.text: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC provide authorization and integrity checks that protect deliverability and reduce spam classification.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.8 › DNS & Deliverability
Definition

SPF, DKIM, DMARC explained

  • SPF — DNS TXT listing authorized sending hosts for a domain.
  • DKIM — cryptographic signing of messages plus a DNS-published public key selector.
  • DMARC — a policy combining SPF and DKIM results with handling instructions and reporting.
Checks
dig TXT example.com
dig MX example.com
# For DKIM, check selector._domainkey.example.com
dig TXT selector._domainkey.example.com
Common misconception: assuming MX and A are sufficient. Missing SPF/DKIM/DMARC often causes downstream filtering even when SMTP succeeds.
Key Takeaway

DNS-based authentication records are critical for mail reputation and acceptance; include them in any delivery checklist.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential commands and concepts you will return to frequently. Journalctl is the systemd journal query tool that surfaces Postfix, Dovecot, and Amavisd events. On some older Red Hat systems /var/log/maillog remains useful, but journalctl is the preferred, structured approach on modern distributions. mailq (or postqueue -p) shows the current message queue and short delivery reasons. Use postconf -n to list only non-default Postfix parameters so you can confirm intentional configuration changes. Telnet and openssl s_client let you reproduce SMTP and IMAP sessions and verify TLS handshakes. SPF, DKIM and DMARC live in DNS; missing records harm deliverability and are outside Postfix configuration but essential for acceptance by remote hosts. Finally, always correlate queue IDs, timestamps, and related service logs when diagnosing—this reduces guesswork and points you to targeted fixes. Keep these concepts at your fingertips when responding to mail incidents.

fullNarratorScript:
Email stacks combine transport, delivery agents, authentication, and filtering. When mail fails, logs and simple client simulations are your fastest path to a root cause. In this lesson you will learn how to read Postfix and Dovecot events, use systemd journal tools to filter mail output, run Postfix utilities to inspect the queue and configuration, and simulate SMTP and IMAP sessions with telnet and openssl. You will also learn why DNS records like MX, A, SPF, DKIM and DMARC matter for deliverability and reputation. Throughout we emphasize practical commands you can run on a server: journalctl, mailq and postqueue, postconf, postlog, telnet, openssl s_client, and dig. You will see a hands-on scenario where a removed mydestination entry causes local delivery to fail, and how logs plus mailq guide the fix. By the end, you will have a checklist you can apply during incidents: locate the right logs, reproduce a session with a client tool, check the queue and configuration, and confirm DNS and filtering services are healthy. Ready to make logs work for you?

By the end of this chapter you will reliably identify where mail events are recorded and why each log matters. You will use journalctl and legacy log files to filter for authentication failures, queue errors and content-filter detections. You will execute Postfix utilities to inspect the mail queue, flush or delete stuck messages, and view non-default configuration parameters so you can compare current state with expected values. You will also simulate SMTP and IMAP interactions using telnet and openssl s_client to reproduce protocol and TLS issues. Each objective maps directly to diagnostic steps: find the right log, reproduce the session, check the queue and config, then verify DNS and filtering services. These skills shorten mean time to resolution and reduce guesswork during incidents. In this screen you will see four competency cards that map an LFCE task to a verified milestone so you can practice with confidence.

These next objectives focus on diagnosing delivery, authentication, and filtering failures and on the DNS records that affect trust and inbox placement. You will be able to diagnose outgoing mail stuck with 'Host not found', by checking resolver configuration and using dig to verify MX and A records. You will diagnose local delivery failures caused by incorrect mydestination settings, reproduce the failure by sending a test message, and correct the configuration to restore delivery. You will inspect Dovecot logs for authentication failures and confirm mailbox paths and permissions. Finally, you will understand why SPF, DKIM, and DMARC belong in your verification checklist: they are outside Postfix configuration yet essential for reputation and acceptance by remote MTAs. Each card includes a small mnemonic or lab target so you can verify your competency in a practical task.

Logs are your primary diagnostic source when mail misbehaves. On systemd-based distributions journalctl is the default interface; older Red Hat systems may still use /var/log/maillog. Postfix prefixes indicate the subsystem generating entries — for example postfix/smtpd shows incoming SMTP activity, postfix/qmgr shows queue operations, and postfix/smtp shows outgoing delivery attempts. Dovecot records authentication and mailbox delivery messages, and Amavisd-new logs provide spam and virus scan results. Start by narrowing time ranges and unit names: sudo journalctl -u postfix -n 50 shows the last 50 Postfix entries and sudo journalctl -u dovecot -n 50 shows recent Dovecot activity. When following live output use -f. A concrete example: if you see status=deferred with a host lookup failure, that points immediately to DNS or network reachability rather than mailbox permissions. A common misconception is scanning maillog for keywords without context; instead, correlate timestamps, queue IDs, and consecutive events to build a timeline of what the MTA tried. Always capture the queue ID from the log and then use mailq to inspect related queue lines. In short, learn the suffixes, use unit filters, and correlate queue IDs to move quickly from symptom to root cause. What timeline will you build on your next incident?

Postfix writes different log prefixes for each subsystem; learning to read those prefixes is critical. postfix/smtpd covers incoming SMTP sessions and command-level responses. When you see rejected connections or authentication errors, smtpd entries are where to start. postfix/qmgr logs queue manager actions such as enqueueing and handing messages to delivery agents. postfix/smtp shows outbound delivery attempts to remote hosts and records SMTP responses from remote MTAs; when you see 4xx or 5xx codes in these entries, they explain why Postfix deferred or bounced mail. postfix/local or postfix/pipe indicate local delivery via the local MTA or an external delivery program like the Dovecot LDA. Practical workflow: reproduce the error, note the queue ID, then run sudo journalctl -u postfix | grep ' ' to gather all related lines. Example commands shown in the visual include tailing the unit and filtering for 'reject' or 'status=deferred'. A misconception is assuming all 'reject' messages are permanent when some are transient 4xx responses; check timestamps and retry behavior. Use the queue ID to link Postfix logs to mailq output and to decide whether to force a queue flush or remove deferred messages. How will you use the queue ID to triangulate the cause on your next ticket?

Dovecot logs give you visibility into authentication, IMAP/POP3 session activity, and local delivery handoffs. When users cannot log in, Dovecot is usually the place to look for exact failure messages such as 'authentication failed' or 'user not found'. Start with sudo journalctl -u dovecot -n 50 and search the output for authentication keywords. Also confirm that the mailbox path exists and permissions are correct; missing or misowned Maildirs will appear as delivery or access errors. A concrete example: a user reports login failures; you grep the dovecot journal and find 'authentication failed' followed by a reason like 'user not found in passwd-file'. That points you toward the authentication backend rather than network issues. A common misconception is to blame the mail client immediately — always verify the server-side authentication log first. For delivery, Dovecot may be invoked as the LDA; check for dovecot-lda handoff messages and any errors indicating mailbox creation or permission denial. After addressing the root cause, test a login with telnet or openssl to reproduce the successful authentication. The key is matching the error text to the authentication backend and mailbox state so you can apply the right fix.

Filtering components sit between Postfix and local delivery; amavisd-new logs reveal whether messages are flagged as spam or infected. If users report missing mail or unexpected quarantines, check amavisd logs: sudo journalctl -u amavisd -n 50 and search for 'SPAM' or virus detections. Filtering failures can be caused by service downtime, misconfigured content_filter entries in Postfix's main. cf or master. cf, or stale virus definitions. A practical check sequence: confirm amavisd, SpamAssassin and ClamAV are running; look for communication entries between Postfix and Amavisd; ensure content filter transport (typically on port 10025) is present. Run freshclam to update virus signatures if ClamAV is out of date. A common misconception is assuming filtering problems always mean spam rules need tweaking — often the issue is an IPC failure between Postfix and the filter or a stopped filter process. Use the logs to see whether messages are passed through, tagged, or rejected, and correlate that with Postfix entries referencing the content_filter transport. When debugging, tail both postfix and amavisd logs together while injecting a test message so you can observe the filter handoff and result in sequence.

Postfix ships utilities that let you inspect current queue state, flush or remove messages, and query configuration. mailq or sudo postqueue -p shows queued messages and the reason for deferral or bounce; you will typically see the queue ID and a short status reason like 'Host not found'. If you must remove deferred mail, postsuper -d ALL deferred clears it — use this cautiously in production. Use sudo postqueue -f to force a queue flush after you fix a network or DNS issue. For configuration, postconf -n shows only non-default settings, which helps you confirm intentional overrides. You can query a single parameter with postconf myhostname, and postconf -d shows default values. postlog is handy when testing scripts or log rotation; it injects a message into Postfix logs so you can confirm log handling. Concrete command examples appear in the code panel: mailq, postqueue -f, postsuper -d ALL deferred, postconf -n and postlog -t mytest. A common misconception is assuming removing deferred mail hides the root cause — always identify why mail deferred before mass-deleting. When you use these tools, capture queue IDs and pair them with journalctl output to create a complete incident timeline.

Manual protocol sessions isolate client-server protocol steps and expose where negotiation fails. For SMTP you can use telnet to port 25 or 587 and type EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA and QUIT to simulate a send. Watch for server responses like 250 OK or 5xx permanent failures. For TLS validation use openssl s_client: openssl s_client -connect mail. example. com:25 -starttls smtp will perform a STARTTLS handshake, letting you inspect the certificate chain and cipher selection. For SMTPS on port 465, use openssl s_client -connect mail. example. com:465 -crlf. For IMAP use telnet to 143 or openssl s_client to 993 for IMAPS. A concrete example: if your client sees a TLS handshake failure, openssl s_client will display certificate errors and the server's presented chain; this confirms whether the issue is client trust or server certificate misconfiguration. A misconception is that telnet hides TLS-related failures — telnet shows cleartext protocol exchange but cannot test STARTTLS unless you then use openssl. Use both tools in sequence: telnet to confirm plain SMTP conversation, then openssl to validate TLS negotiation. When you simulate commands, record the exact server responses and correlate them to the Postfix logs to complete the diagnostic loop.

When outgoing messages show 'Host not found' in the queue, Postfix cannot resolve the recipient's mail host. The most likely cause is a DNS resolver issue on the mail server. Immediate steps: check /etc/resolv. conf for valid nameserver entries, test DNS with dig MX recipient_domain. com and dig A mail. recipient_domain. com from the mail host, and confirm network connectivity to your configured DNS servers. Also check firewall rules that might block outbound DNS queries or SMTP connections. In practice, reproduce the failure by sending a message, run mailq to capture the queue ID and reason, then inspect journalctl -u postfix for matching lines that show name resolution failure. If DNS resolution succeeds from the server but Postfix still shows host lookup failures, verify that chroot or containerized environments have access to resolv. conf and that DNS is reachable from the Postfix process. A misconception is to assume Postfix is misconfigured; often the resolver is unreachable or mis-specified. After fixing resolv. conf or network access, run postqueue -f to retry deliveries. This stepwise approach isolates network/DNS versus MTA configuration issues and guides a targeted fix.

When a user cannot log in, you must decide whether the problem originates on the server or in the client. Server-side signs include 'authentication failed' or 'user not found' in Dovecot logs, missing Maildir directories, or incorrect ownership and permissions on mailbox paths. Client-side signs can include authentication errors only from a single client or unusual client-side TLS errors. A practical path: check Dovecot logs first for explicit reasons; if logs say user not found, inspect password backends and virtual user files. If logs show permission denied, inspect Maildir paths and fix ownership. If the server log shows nothing, reproduce the login via telnet or openssl s_client while tailing the dovecot journal to capture the server's reaction. Also check disable_plaintext_auth settings and TLS requirements; some clients fail if plaintext auth is disabled without TLS. A common misconception is to reset the user's password before verifying the actual failure reason; instead, gather evidence from logs and simulate the authentication to confirm the root cause. Finish by testing a successful login and confirming delivery or mailbox listing to validate the repair. Beyond MX and A records, SPF, DKIM and DMARC play a decisive role in whether your mail is accepted or marked as spam. SPF is a DNS TXT record that lists which hosts are allowed to send mail for your domain; it helps recipient servers quickly determine if a sending IP is authorized. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages so the recipient can verify the email's origin and integrity using a published public key. DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM by declaring a policy that tells receivers what to do when a message fails authentication and allows you to request reports. These records are not configured inside Postfix or Dovecot directly but are essential verification checkpoints for remote MTAs. A common misconception is treating these as optional; without them your outgoing mail is more likely to be soft- or hard-rejected or silently routed to spam. Practical checks include dig TXT example. com to find SPF or DKIM selectors and verifying that DKIM public keys match the signing selector. If delivery fails despite correct MTA logs, confirm these DNS records with the receiving domain’s rejection messages. In short: DNS proves who you are; ensure these records are present and correct as part of your incident checklist.

Let's summarize the essential commands and concepts you will return to frequently. Journalctl is the systemd journal query tool that surfaces Postfix, Dovecot, and Amavisd events. On some older Red Hat systems /var/log/maillog remains useful, but journalctl is the preferred, structured approach on modern distributions. mailq (or postqueue -p) shows the current message queue and short delivery reasons. Use postconf -n to list only non-default Postfix parameters so you can confirm intentional configuration changes. Telnet and openssl s_client let you reproduce SMTP and IMAP sessions and verify TLS handshakes. SPF, DKIM and DMARC live in DNS; missing records harm deliverability and are outside Postfix configuration but essential for acceptance by remote hosts. Finally, always correlate queue IDs, timestamps, and related service logs when diagnosing—this reduces guesswork and points you to targeted fixes. Keep these concepts at your fingertips when responding to mail incidents.
